svg.text: The postnatal period: where the deaths actually happen
Most maternal and newborn deaths occur in the first 24 hours and the first week — not during the birth itself.
First 24 hours
Day 3
Day 7 to 14
Six weeks
Four postnatal contacts, whether she gave birth in a facility or at home.
Checking the mother
Uterus: firm, and descending about a
centimetre a day — impalpable by day 10
Lochia: rubra to serosa to alba
Temperature, pulse, blood pressure
Breasts, perineum, legs
Mood — ask directly, every visit
Bladder full? The uterus rises and deviates.
Maternal danger signs
Heavy bleeding — soaking a pad in 5 minutes
Fever, or foul-smelling lochia
Severe headache or visual disturbance
Convulsions — eclampsia still happens after birth
Calf pain, swelling, breathlessness
Thoughts of harming herself or the baby
A uterus that is high, soft and boggy is refilling.
Puerperal sepsis — the classic pattern
Fever with a tender, poorly contracted uterus and offensive lochia, usually from day 2 onwards.
Risk rises with prolonged rupture of membranes, repeated vaginal examinations, retained products and unclean birth.
Take cultures, start broad antibiotics without waiting for results, and hunt for retained products.
Mood, and the distinction that matters
Baby blues: days 3 to 5, tearful, resolves within two weeks, needs support and no treatment.
Depression: persists beyond two weeks, affects function and bonding, needs treatment.
Psychosis: confusion, delusions, thoughts of harm — a psychiatric emergency, admit with the baby if possible.
